blocks.html: Vinorama Fishing Guide — San Jose del Cabo
Explore Vinorama fishing near San Jose del Cabo: yellowfin tuna, live-bait tactics, dorado, sharks and changing seasonal conditions in the Sea of Cortez.

Vinorama is one of the best-documented yellowfin tuna fishing areas near San Jose del Cabo. Regional fishing reports show everything from productive live-bait sessions to exceptionally difficult days affected by sharks, currents and changing fish activity.

For anglers interested in yellowfin tuna, understanding these fluctuations is just as important as knowing the name of the fishing ground.

Vinorama is also associated with dorado, occasional wahoo and opportunities to explore nearby rocky structures for bottom fish.

Where Is Vinorama Fishing Ground?

Vinorama is located northeast of San Jose del Cabo along the Sea of Cortez fishing grounds.

It is frequently mentioned alongside San Luis, Iman Bank and Cardon in regional fishing reports.

Anglers may focus on Vinorama when yellowfin tuna are active or cover neighboring grounds when feeding activity becomes unpredictable.

Fishing conditions can change between one day and the next, so the most recent regional observations are an important consideration when selecting a destination.

Yellowfin Tuna — The Main Attraction at Vinorama

Yellowfin tuna are the principal species associated with many Vinorama fishing reports.

During late May 2026, regional reports described yellowfin tuna weighing mostly 10–20 pounds around Vinorama and San Luis, with some larger 30–40-pound fish encountered in the same area.

The bite was productive early in that week before increasing shark activity reduced the number of successful landings.

In August 2026, the fishing picture changed again.

A report covering August 3–11 documented yellowfin tuna of approximately 20–80 pounds around Vinorama. Live sardines were the main bait, and tuna activity improved as the reporting period progressed.

However, sharks continued to interfere with many hookups.

By September, fishing had become more unpredictable.

On September 13, 2026, the regional report described a slower tuna bite, with some outings fortunate to hook only one or two yellowfin.

A week later, a 280-pound yellowfin was reported landed by an independent commercial fishing operation at Vinorama.

That exceptional catch demonstrates the possibility of large fish, but it should not be confused with a typical daily result.

Live Bait, Sardines and Tuna Techniques

Live sardines have been one of the most important baits documented in Vinorama reports.

When sardines are available, anglers may use them to attract feeding yellowfin and present bait to active fish.

However, bait supply is not always reliable.

The September 20, 2026, report described increasingly scarce live sardines, with some outings switching to dead sardines and frozen squid.

Regional reports have also documented live caballito and bulito being used to target larger fish.

The effective bait can change according to size, availability and how the tuna are feeding.

Why Sharks Matter at Vinorama

One of the most important lessons from the 2026 fishing reports is the difference between hooking yellowfin tuna and successfully landing them.

Shark interference repeatedly affected Vinorama from late spring through September.

During some outings, sharks took hooked fish before they could reach the boat.

Longer fights with larger tuna sometimes increased the chance of interference.

This means a report describing active yellowfin or multiple hookups does not necessarily indicate that the same number of tuna were landed.

Vinorama can offer exciting fishing opportunities while remaining unpredictable in practical terms.

Dorado, Wahoo and Bottom Fishing

Yellowfin tuna are not the only species documented around Vinorama.

Regional reports from August 2026 mention dorado caught while using live sardines for tuna and while trolling small lures or rigged ballyhoo toward Cardon.

One August report also documented a wahoo weighing approximately 25 pounds caught on live sardines in the Vinorama area.

Bottom-fishing attempts have produced leopard grouper, snapper and other species, although strong current and sharks sometimes made those techniques difficult.

The available reports therefore support describing Vinorama as a mixed fishing ground, with yellowfin tuna as its principal documented attraction.

What Is the Best Time to Fish Vinorama?

There is no single month that guarantees good tuna fishing at Vinorama.

Regional reports document activity in spring, summer and early fall, but the catch patterns vary considerably.

For example:

  • May 2026: Active small yellowfin early in the week, followed by increasing shark interference.

  • August 2026: Yellowfin commonly reported in the 20–80-pound range during one reporting period, with variable landing success.

  • September 2026: Slower, less consistent fishing despite reports of some very large tuna.

These are historical examples, not a forecast for future trips.

Current bait, water conditions, shark activity and port status should guide the fishing plan.

Vinorama vs. Iman Bank and San Luis

Vinorama frequently appears in reports focused on yellowfin tuna.

Iman Bank is another important tuna area, but its regional reports also contain numerous examples of productive snapper and grouper fishing.

San Luis provides access to rocky bottom structure and nearby shorelines where roosterfish and other coastal species have been reported.

Anglers who want a flexible experience may prefer a fishing plan that can change location when the bite slows.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Vinorama good for yellowfin tuna?

Vinorama has a substantial history of reported yellowfin tuna activity, but catches can be inconsistent and shark interference can be significant.

What bait is used for tuna at Vinorama?

Historical reports describe live sardines, caballito and other baitfish, along with dead sardines and squid when live bait is unavailable.

Can you catch dorado or wahoo at Vinorama?

Yes. Both species have been documented around Vinorama and adjacent trolling grounds, although reported catches are less consistent than yellowfin tuna activity.
